clue.text: His works are rarely read (never even scanned)

definitions.text: His works are rarely read (never even scanned)

parts.words: His works are rarely read (never even scanned)
parts.note: the clue describes a Victorian Scottish versifier famous as the worst poet in the language, whose lines notoriously fail to scan; 'scanned' also means glanced over

explanation.surface: A neglected author whose books nobody even glances at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scanned' looks like 'skimmed', but it is the metrical sense: William McGonagall of Dundee wrote verse with no regular metre at all.
explanation.definitionFit: William McGonagall is the celebrated bad poet whose doggerel ignores metre and is read now mostly for laughs.

clue.text: Sign, say, of village poet

indicators.note: say tells us to pronounce the word for the sign and hear the poet's name

parts.note: the zodiac sign Cancer is the crab

explanation.surface: Asking what omen marks a rustic bard.
explanation.walkthrough: George Crabbe wrote the poem 'The Village' (1783), a bleak picture of rural life, so 'village poet' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: George Crabbe is the Suffolk poet best known for his realistic poem of country life, 'The Village'.

clue.text: Unknown dimwit follows up neat combination of contradictory terms

indicators.note: follows up places the following pieces after the cattle in this down entry

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, of which an ox is one
in algebra an unknown quantity is written x, y or z; here Y
a dimwit is a moron

explanation.surface: A stranger, a fool, trails behind a tidy blend of opposing words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' reads as tidy, but it is the archaic word for cattle; 'follows up' suits a down clue, the fool coming below the beast.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech such as 'deafening silence' yokes together words of opposite meaning.

clue.text: A haul Acton possibly offers of syntactic non sequiturs

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the preceding words may be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Lord Acton, the historian, perhaps hauls in a load of broken sentences.
explanation.walkthrough: A is given as it is; 'possibly' rearranges HAUL ACTON into NACOLUTHA.
explanation.definitionFit: These are sentences that break off and continue with a grammatically different construction, a rhetorical term from Greek.

clue.text: A doctor was elevated for Scott's father.

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
was elevated means rose

explanation.surface: A physician got a promotion on behalf of Sir Walter Scott's parent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Scott's actual father; it is Father Ambrose, the abbot in Scott's novels 'The Monastery' and 'The Abbot'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Walter Scott's 'The Abbot', the monk Edward Glendinning becomes Father Ambrose, a priest called father.

clue.text: … while Marina Warner's was apparently mislaid

definitions.text: while Marina Warner's was apparently mislaid

parts.words: while Marina Warner's was apparently mislaid
parts.note: continuing the previous clue's 'father', Marina Warner's novel is titled The ___ Father, so her father seems to have gone missing

explanation.surface: Carrying on from Scott's father, the novelist's own parent went missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries 'father' over from 5-down: Marina Warner's 1988 novel is 'The Lost Father'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mislaid has gone missing, and Warner's book title applies that adjective to a parent.

clue.text: Source of O'Neill play

explanation.definitionFit: A spring is a source of water, and Eugene O'Neill wrote a 1925 play about Ponce de León's quest for the water of youth with this title.

clue.text: Descendant of presidents whose education was an open book

definitions.text: Descendant of presidents whose education was an open book

parts.words: Descendant of presidents whose education was an open book
parts.note: the grandson and great-grandson of two US presidents wrote an autobiography titled The Education of ..., so his schooling literally became a published book

explanation.surface: A child of a political dynasty with nothing hidden about how he was taught.
explanation.definitionFit: The American historian, grandson of John Quincy Adams, wrote the celebrated memoir 'The Education of Henry Adams'.

clue.text: Mythical singer of I Love Paris?

definitions.text: Mythical singer of I Love Paris?

parts.words: Mythical singer of I Love Paris?
parts.note: the Cole Porter song title is read as a lament by the nymph who was Paris of Troy's first wife and was deserted by him for Helen; Tennyson gave her a poem of complaint

explanation.surface: Which legendary vocalist performed the Cole Porter standard?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paris' looks like the French capital, but it is the Trojan prince who abandoned this nymph; Tennyson's poem gives her lament.
explanation.definitionFit: Oenone, the mountain nymph of Ida, loved and married the shepherd prince before he left her for Helen.

clue.text: Children's writer, had a little missing from well-known rhyme

indicators.note: missing tells us the quoted words are taken out of the rhyme's title

parts.note: the nursery rhyme 'Mary Had a Little Lamb'

explanation.surface: An author for children owned a small one, absent from a famous verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove 'had a little' from the title of the nursery rhyme to leave the name of Charles Lamb's sister, co-author of 'Tales from Shakespeare'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Lamb wrote 'Tales from Shakespeare' for young readers with her brother Charles.

clue.text: Newfangled art Irene supplied servant

indicators.note: newfangled means remade in a new fashion, so the letters of art and Irene are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Irene's modern art paid for her household help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newfangled' rearranges ART IRENE.
explanation.definitionFit: A retainer is an old word for a servant attached to a household, especially a long-serving one.

clue.text: The legatee of Vita Sackville-West

parts.note: Vita Sackville-West wrote a 1922 novella of this title about a man who inherits a house; the word means one who receives a legacy

explanation.surface: Who inherited from the Bloomsbury writer?
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as asking who inherited from Vita Sackville-West, but it names her novella 'The Heir'.
explanation.definitionFit: A legatee is a person who inherits property, and Sackville-West's book takes that word for its title.

clue.text: Herrick's three sisters

explanation.definitionFit: Robert Herrick's 1648 poetry collection bears this title, and in Greek myth these nymphs, often three sisters, guarded the golden apples.

clue.text: Possibly sly one, with several layers, as Greek peacemaker

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of sly may be rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
strata are layers, as of rock

explanation.surface: A cunning sort with many levels plays the role of a Greek who brings peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' turns SLY into LYS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Aristophanes's comedy, the Athenian heroine ends the war by leading a sex strike among the women.

clue.text: He was to be seen in the company of Vincent Crummles

definitions.text: He was to be seen in the company of Vincent Crummles

parts.words: He was to be seen in the company of Vincent Crummles
parts.note: the 'company' is Crummles's touring theatre troupe in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby; a member of it was literally on view to audiences

explanation.surface: Someone spotted alongside a theatrical manager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' reads as companionship but is the acting company; Mr Snevellicci is an actor in it and the father of Miss Snevellicci.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'Nicholas Nickleby' the Snevellicci family are players in the Crummles troupe that Nicholas joins.

clue.text: Boy secures verses

parts.note: a boy is a son
nets means secures, as in netting a deal

explanation.surface: A lad gets hold of some poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonnets are fourteen-line poems, so they are pieces of verse.

clue.text: "And we have built Jerusalem", he may well have claimed

definitions.text: "And we have built Jerusalem", he may well have claimed

parts.words: "And we have built Jerusalem", he may well have claimed
parts.note: echoing Blake's hymn line about building Jerusalem, this points to the Old Testament governor who rebuilt the city's walls; 'well' hints at 'wall'

explanation.surface: A singer of Blake's hymn boasts that the job is done.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake's 'Jerusalem' (sung as a hymn in Britain) has 'Till we have built Jerusalem'; the Book of Nehemiah tells how he led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Nehemiah was the Persian king's cupbearer who returned to Judah and organised the rebuilding of the city walls.

clue.text: Eastern philosophy to some extent braved antagonism

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone partly faced down hostility to Oriental thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to some extent' points to the letters inside bra(VED ANTA)gonism.
explanation.definitionFit: Vedanta is a school of Hindu thought based on the Upanishads.

clue.text: M.R. James issued one to the curious

definitions.text: M.R. James issued one to the curious

parts.words: M.R. James issued one to the curious
parts.note: the ghost-story writer's tale is titled with a caution addressed to inquisitive people

explanation.surface: The antiquarian author cautioned nosy people.
explanation.walkthrough: M.R. James's ghost story 'A Warning to the Curious' (1925) is built into the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A caution given in advance is the thing James's title offers to inquisitive readers.

clue.text: Stanzas offering everything in incorrect English

indicators.note: in puts the word for everything inside the word for incorrect

parts.note: incorrect means bad
everything means all

explanation.surface: Verses that deliver the lot in faulty English.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballade is a French verse form of three stanzas and an envoi, so the word stands for a set of verses.

clue.text: "Peregrine… advised him to his spirits with a glass of wine " (Smollett)

definitions.text: "Peregrine… advised him to his spirits with a glass of wine " (Smollett)

parts.words: "Peregrine… advised him to his spirits with a glass of wine " (Smollett)
parts.note: a quotation from Smollett's Peregrine Pickle with a verb missing after 'to': the word needed means to cheer or enliven

explanation.surface: A line from Smollett where a friend recommends wine to lift someone's mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Supply the missing word in 'advised him to ___ his spirits'; the gap is the clue, from Tobias Smollett's novel 'Peregrine Pickle'.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise someone's spirits is to make them cheerful, which a glass of wine is advised to do.

clue.text: A student with degree, in vestments

parts.note: L, the learner plate, stands for a student
BS, Bachelor of Science, is a degree

explanation.surface: A graduate dressed in robes.
explanation.walkthrough: L (learner) is the crossword student, from the L-plates a British learner driver displays.
explanation.definitionFit: Albs are white linen tunics worn by clergy at the altar, a kind of liturgical robe.

clue.text: He was translated for a queen

definitions.text: He was translated for a queen

parts.words: He was translated for a queen
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream, Quince cries that the weaver is 'translated' when given an ass's head, and Titania the fairy queen falls for him

explanation.surface: A text rendered into another language for royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translated' looks literary but is Shakespeare's sense 'transformed': the weaver Bottom gets an ass's head and Titania dotes on him.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottom the weaver is the character changed into an ass's form and loved by the bewitched Fairy Queen.

clue.text: Enduring, like Victor Hugo or Marguerite Yourcenar, for example

definitions.text: like Victor Hugo or Marguerite Yourcenar, for example

explanation.definitionFit: Something enduring lasts forever, and members of the Académie française, such as Hugo and Yourcenar, its first woman member, are nicknamed 'les immortels'.

clue.text: In short, William Golding's seamen's argot

definitions.text: In short, William Golding's seamen's argot

indicators.note: in short means the word is abbreviated, cut down to its familiar short form

parts.note: in Golding's sea trilogy beginning Rites of Passage, the narrator calls the sailors' jargon 'tarpaulin'

explanation.surface: Summing up the sailors' slang in Golding's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' cuts the sea-language word, Talbot's name for sailor-talk in Golding's 'Rites of Passage', to its everyday short form.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarp is a waterproof canvas sheet, and the full word also named a sailor, whose speech Golding's narrator calls by it.

clue.text: Believers in a vital force, like Plato, Pythagoras, Disney perhaps?

explanation.definitionFit: Animism attributes a soul to things, as the world-soul of Plato and Pythagoras; Disney's animators brought drawings to life.

clue.text: AE errs badly? may employ this

definitions.text: AE errs badly? may employ this

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the preceding words are mixed up

explanation.surface: If the Irish poet AE makes a bad slip, he may reach for a rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges AE ERRS; AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who makes a written mistake uses a rubber to remove it, so the whole clue describes the tool.

clue.text: Turgid versifications including one's Reminiscences

parts.note: McGonagall's collected doggerel was published under an ironically grand title, with the author's Reminiscences included

explanation.surface: A bombastic verse collection padded out with memoirs.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital R points to the volume of McGonagall's verse (see 1-across) that included his 'Reminiscences'.
explanation.definitionFit: McGonagall's collected verse bore this boastful title, which ironically calls his clumsy poems precious jewels.
